lesson.title: Sinners, Spiders, and Salvation: Jonathan Edwards and the Theology of Revival
lesson.summary: Jonathan Edwards, a Massachusetts minister and one of colonial America's most rigorous theologians, both sparked local revivals and gave the Great Awakening its intellectual foundation and most famous sermon.
lesson.body:
Jonathan Edwards was born in 1703 in East Windsor, Connecticut, the son of a minister, and he grew into one of the most intellectually serious theologians colonial America produced. He entered Yale College at a young age, studied the philosophy of John Locke and the science of Isaac Newton alongside traditional Calvinist theology, and eventually took over the pulpit in Northampton, Massachusetts, a church previously led by his grandfather, Solomon Stoddard. Edwards was not simply an emotional preacher. He was a careful thinker who tried to explain, in rigorous philosophical terms, why a genuine religious conversion changed a person's whole perception of the world.

Edwards's own congregation experienced a local revival in 1734 and 1735, sometimes called the Northampton awakening, in which dozens of townspeople reported sudden, intense conversion experiences. Edwards wrote a detailed account of these events that circulated in print and helped inspire the broader colonial revivals that became known as the Great Awakening. When George Whitefield toured New England in 1740, Edwards welcomed him to preach in Northampton, and the two men, different in temperament but united in purpose, became linked in the public mind as leaders of the movement.

Edwards's most famous sermon, Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God, was delivered in the summer of 1741 in the town of Enfield. Using vivid imagery, Edwards described unconverted sinners as suspended over the fires of hell by a thin thread, held back only by God's mercy, in language meant to shock listeners into recognizing their spiritual danger. The sermon is remembered today as the defining literary artifact of the Great Awakening precisely because it captures, in dramatic form, the movement's core claim that ordinary religious observance was not enough and that individuals needed a direct, felt encounter with divine judgment and grace.

Edwards eventually paid a price for his rigor. His grandfather Stoddard had allowed a wider circle of townspeople to take communion as a way of drawing them closer to full conversion, a practice sometimes called the halfway covenant tradition. Edwards came to believe communion should be reserved only for those who could demonstrate a genuine conversion experience, and this stricter standard angered his congregation. In 1750 Northampton voted to dismiss him from the pulpit his family had held for decades.

After his dismissal, Edwards moved to the frontier town of Stockbridge, Massachusetts, where he served as a missionary to Mohican and other Native American communities while continuing to write major theological works. In early 1758 he accepted the presidency of the College of New Jersey, the school that later became Princeton, but he died within weeks of arriving, in March 1758, from complications following a smallpox inoculation. Edwards left behind a body of theology and, through Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God, an enduring symbol of the Great Awakening's power to unsettle comfortable religion and demand a more personal, urgent faith.
